---
title: "9. Alignment of relative data measurements"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, dpi = 96,
                      fig.retina = 2, message = FALSE)
```

Western blots, plate readers and many other assays give readings on a scale of their own: one
gel is exposed longer than the next, one plate has a higher background. Before such data enter a
dynamic model, or instead of it, the readings of all experiments are brought onto one common
scale. `alignmentModel()` and `align()` do this by maximum likelihood, with the model of a
reading written as an expression, as in blotIt.

```{r}
library(dMod2)
library(ggplot2)
options(dMod2.outdir = file.path(tempdir(), "guide-alignment"))
dir.create(getOption("dMod2.outdir"), showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## Data

A phosphorylation after stimulation at five time points, in six biological replicates: six
independent experiments, each with its own cells, stimulation and lysates, blotted on a gel of
its own. Every sample runs in three lanes of its gel, its technical replicates. The simulation
draws the level of every sample around the true course with a biological variability of 20 %,
an exposure and a background for every gel, and a technical noise of 15 % for every lane.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
times <- c(0, 10, 30, 60, 120)
truth <- c(0.3, 1, 4, 2, 0.5)
gels <- paste0("G", 1:6)
samples <- expand.grid(time = times, gel = gels, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
samples$level <- truth[match(samples$time, times)] * rlnorm(nrow(samples), 0, 0.2)
scale <- setNames(rlnorm(6, 7, 0.5), gels)
background <- setNames(rlnorm(6, log(100), 0.3), gels)
lane <- rep(seq_len(nrow(samples)), each = 3)
d <- data.frame(samples[lane, c("time", "gel")], lane = 1:3, row.names = NULL)
d$value <- (scale[d$gel] * samples$level[lane] + background[d$gel]) * rlnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.15)
head(d)
```

## Model

A reading is a biological value `yi` times the scale `sj` of its gel plus a background `bj`,
with a standard deviation proportional to the prediction. Every symbol of the expressions is a
linear predictor over the columns of the data, set by a formula per role: one value per time
point, one scale per gel, one background and one error parameter for all. The transformation puts
every symbol on a log scale, so all of them stay positive. `technical = "lane"` replaces the
three lanes of every sample by their mean, see
[technical and biological replicates](#technical-and-biological-replicates).

```{r}
logs <- c("yi <- exp(yi)", "sj <- exp(sj)", "bj <- exp(bj)", "sigmaR <- exp(sigmaR)")
m <- alignmentModel(d, model = "yi * sj + bj", errmodel = "sigmaR * prediction",
                    biological = yi ~ time, scaling = sj ~ gel, error = bj + sigmaR ~ 1, trafo = logs,
                    technical = "lane")
m
```

Values and scales share a common factor: doubling every value and halving every scale changes
nothing. The alignment fixes it by holding the geometric mean of the values at 1, within every
block of experiments that share values.

## Fit

`align()` fits from several perturbed starts and keeps the best. The error parameters are
estimated by restricted maximum likelihood by default, which corrects them for the degrees of
freedom the parameters of the prediction take from the data, many in an alignment: here 5
values, 6 scales and the background against 30 readings. The print says which likelihood the
$-2 \log L$ of the fit is, and lists the maximum likelihood fits the restricted one starts from.

```{r}
fit <- align(m, fits = 4)
fit
```

The aligned values, with standard errors, are the result:

```{r}
fit$aligned
```

## Estimates against the truth

On the scale of the alignment, with the geometric mean of the values at 1, the simulated course
is `truth / exp(mean(log(truth)))`. The error of an aligned value, the log of its ratio to the
simulated one, against its standard error `se` on the same scale:

```{r}
simulated <- data.frame(time = times, value = truth / exp(mean(log(truth))))
errors <- function(fit) {
  a <- fit$aligned[match(times, fit$aligned$time), ]
  data.frame(time = times, simulated = simulated$value, aligned = a$value,
             error = log(a$value / simulated$value), se = a$se)
}
signif(errors(fit), 2)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(fit$aligned, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = value - sigma, ymax = value + sigma), width = 0) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "aligned")) +
  geom_point(data = simulated, aes(shape = "simulated"), size = 2.5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(aligned = 16, simulated = 4), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "time [min]", y = "value") + theme_dMod()
```

## Technical and biological replicates

A biological replicate repeats the experiment: other cells, another stimulation, another
lysate. Its readings differ from those of the other replicates by the biological variability
of the response and by every step of the measurement. A technical replicate measures the same
sample again: the same lysate in another lane, the same cDNA in another well. Its readings
differ from those of the other technical replicates by the steps of the measurement alone.

The lanes of one sample share its biological deviation: when the sample holds 20 % more of the
phosphoprotein than the mean, all three lanes show it. They are three readings of one sample,
not three independent readings of the biology. `technical = "lane"` averages them to one reading
per sample before the alignment: readings that agree in all columns but `value`,
`lloq` and the technical columns are one sample. With a relative error model, as here, the mean
is geometric, taken on the log scale; with an absolute one, as for readings on a log scale
already, it is arithmetic. The error model then describes the scatter of the sample means,
the biological variability and the technical noise of the mean of three lanes together.

The same data with every lane counted as a reading of its own:

```{r}
mLanes <- alignmentModel(d, model = "yi * sj + bj", errmodel = "sigmaR * prediction",
                         biological = yi ~ time, scaling = sj ~ gel, error = bj + sigmaR ~ 1,
                         trafo = logs)
fitLanes <- align(mLanes, fits = 4)
fitLanes
signif(errors(fitLanes), 2)
```

Both fits find nearly the same values with the same errors. The fit of the lanes reports
standard errors smaller by about the square root of 3, the number of lanes per sample: it
counts 90 readings, but most of the error of a value is the biological deviation of the
samples, of which there are 30. Its errors reach 1.7 standard errors, those of the fit of
the means stay within one.

## Background per gel

When the background differs between gels but six free backgrounds would cost too many degrees of
freedom, it can vary as a random effect: one background per gel, drawn around a common value. A
role then takes a list of formulas, and the fit integrates the random effects by FOCEI as in
[chapter 7](guide-nlme.html), with the standard deviation of the backgrounds estimated by
restricted likelihood. Five readings per gel say little about how much the backgrounds differ, so
a prior keeps the standard deviation of the log background near 0.3, its log `omega_bj_bj` normal
around $\log 0.3$ with standard deviation 0.3.

```{r}
m2 <- alignmentModel(d, model = "yi * sj + bj", errmodel = "sigmaR * prediction",
                     biological = yi ~ time, scaling = list(sj ~ gel, bj ~ 1 + (1 | gel)),
                     error = sigmaR ~ 1, trafo = logs, technical = "lane",
                     prior = constraintL2(mu = c(omega_bj_bj = log(0.3)), sigma = 0.3))
fit2 <- align(m2, fits = 4)
fit2
signif(errors(fit2), 2)
```

The background of every gel, the common one times its random effect at the mode, against the
simulated one:

```{r}
bg <- exp(fit2$parameters[["bj"]] + fit2$random$mode[match(gels, fit2$random$group)])
data.frame(gel = gels, simulated = round(background), common = round(exp(fit$parameters[["bj"]])),
           random = round(bg))
```

The two fits have nearly the same likelihood, and the values change by less than their
standard errors. The random backgrounds lie below the simulated ones, with little spread
around their common value: the bands of these gels lie far above the background and say
little about it. In the [Western blots](#western-blot-and-targeted-mass-spectrometry) below, gels
with weak lanes resolve it.

## Options

| argument | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `fits` | `10` | fits from perturbed starts |
| `sd` | `0.5` | standard deviation of the perturbation |
| `reml` | `TRUE` | error parameters and random-effect spreads by restricted likelihood |
| `method` | `"focei"` | with random terms, `"focei"` or `"quadrature"` |
| `cores` | `1` | fits in parallel |

The objective of an alignment needs no ODE solver and is exact up to rounding: the fits stop at
changes, predicted decreases and gradients below the square root of the machine precision.

Readings on an absolute scale, such as concentrations from targeted mass spectrometry, are marked
in a column `absolute` and fix the scale of the blocks they belong to. The two sections below
align real assay designs: qPCR experiments with wells below the detection limit, and Western
blots with a random background per gel together with targeted mass spectrometry in nM.

## qPCR

The mRNA of a target gene after stimulation at seven time points, measured in four experiments,
the biological replicates, every sample in two wells, technical duplicates. Each experiment has
its own cells, cDNA and plate and a subset of the time points; no time point is in every
experiment. A well reports the cycle Ct at which its fluorescence crosses a threshold, a level set
above the background while the signal still grows exponentially. The amount doubles with every
cycle, so 36 - Ct is the log2 concentration in arbitrary units, shifted by an offset of the
experiment. Untreated cells barely express the target: a well that has not crossed the threshold
after 40 cycles reports no Ct, and its reading lies below 36 - 40 = -4.

### Data

The column `lloq` holds the limit of every reading; a reading `NA` is censored there. The
samples differ from the course of their experiment by 0.5 cycles (standard deviation), the
two wells of a sample by 0.25.

```{r}
set.seed(5)
times <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 24)
log2fold <- c(0, 0.3, 1.6, 3.6, 5.2, 5.6, 4.4)
runs <- list(E1 = times[1:6], E2 = times[c(1, 3:5, 7)], E3 = times[c(2, 3, 6, 7)], E4 = times[c(1, 2, 4:7)])
samples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(runs), function(e) data.frame(experiment = e, time = runs[[e]])))
offset <- setNames(rnorm(length(runs)), names(runs))
samples$ct <- 39.3 - log2fold[match(samples$time, times)] - offset[samples$experiment] +
  rnorm(nrow(samples), 0, 0.5)
well <- rep(seq_len(nrow(samples)), each = 2)
qpcr <- data.frame(samples[well, c("experiment", "time")], well = 1:2, row.names = NULL)
ct <- samples$ct[well] + rnorm(nrow(qpcr), 0, 0.25)
qpcr$value <- ifelse(ct < 40, 36 - ct, NA)
qpcr$lloq <- -4
head(qpcr)
sum(is.na(qpcr$value))
```

### Model

The reading is `yi + sj`: `yi` the log2 concentration per time point, `sj` the offset of
the experiment. The error is absolute. The two wells of a sample are averaged,
`technical = "well"`; the readings are on the log2 scale already, and with an absolute
error model the mean is arithmetic. A sample with a well below the limit is censored at the
mean of the other well and the limit, which its mean lies below.

```{r}
m <- alignmentModel(qpcr, model = "yi + sj", errmodel = "sigma",
                    biological = yi ~ time,
                    scaling    = sj ~ experiment,
                    error      = sigma ~ 1,
                    trafo = "sigma <- exp(sigma)", technical = "well")
m
```

### Fit

The mean of the values is held at 0, so they are log2 concentrations relative to their
mean. Their differences to the untreated value are the log2 fold changes.

```{r}
fit <- align(m, fits = 1)
fit
a <- fit$aligned
a$log2fc <- a$estimate - a$estimate[a$time == 0]
cbind(a[c("time", "estimate", "se", "log2fc")], simulated = log2fold[match(a$time, times)])
```

The readings of every experiment, the means of the duplicates, before and after the
alignment. A censored sample has no reading; it enters the fit by its limit and is not drawn.

```{r}
s <- fit$scaled[!fit$scaled$bloq, ]
both <- rbind(data.frame(s[c("experiment", "time")], stage = "before", value = s$value),
              data.frame(s[c("experiment", "time")], stage = "after", value = s$scaled))
both$stage <- factor(both$stage, c("before", "after"))
```
```{r fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(both, aes(factor(time), value, colour = experiment)) +
  geom_point() + facet_wrap(~ stage) +
  labs(x = "time [h]", y = "log2(conc.) [a.u.]", colour = "experiment") +
  scale_color_dMod() + theme_dMod()

```
```{r fig.height = 3.5}
plotAligned(fit) + scale_x_sqrt(breaks = times) + labs(x = "time [h]", y = "log2(conc.) [a.u.]")
```
```{r fig.height = 3}
plotResiduals(fit)
```

### Aligned values in a model fit

```{r}
as.datalist(fit)
```

## Western blot and targeted mass spectrometry

A phosphoprotein after stimulation with a ligand, quantified on ten gels and by targeted
mass spectrometry. Five gels hold a short time course up to 4 h, five a long one up to
48 h; the two courses share only the untreated lane and 4 h. Every gel holds four of the
time points of its course and is imaged on a scale of its own, the long gels far lower
on the whole. A gel adds its own background to the bands, the signal of the membrane
around them, and its image scales both. The background shows on gels with weak lanes,
the untreated one and the late ones, and hides under the bands of the others. With a
background of its own on every gel, the untreated level and the typical background are
told apart only by how the background varies between gels: a normal random effect per
gel. The mass spectrometry measures the concentration in nM at four time points of both
courses, three samples each. Its readings are absolute: marked in the column `absolute`, they
are predicted by the expression `absolute`, by default the first biological symbol, and
depend on no scaling parameter. Their gel is `NA`. The block of experiments they belong
to is not normalised but comes out in nM.

### Data

One row per reading, log2 of the band in arbitrary units or of the concentration in nM.
The gels of the short course are S1 to S5, those of the long one L1 to L5.

```{r}
set.seed(6)
short <- c(0, 10, 30, 60, 120, 240)
long <- c(0, 240, 480, 1440, 2880)
times <- sort(union(short, long))
conc <- c(1, 40, 85, 60, 25, 10, 6, 3, 2)
gels <- c(sprintf("S%d", 1:5), sprintf("L%d", 1:5))
course <- setNames(rep(c("short", "long"), each = 5), gels)
shift <- setNames(ifelse(course == "short", 6, 1) + rnorm(10, 0, 1.5), gels)
background <- setNames(1.5 + rnorm(10, 0, 0.3), gels)
wb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gels, function(g)
  data.frame(method = "WB", gel = g, time = sort(sample(if (course[[g]] == "short") short else long, 4)))))
wb$value <- log2(conc[match(wb$time, times)] + 2^background[wb$gel]) + shift[wb$gel] +
  rnorm(nrow(wb), 0, 0.7)
ms <- data.frame(method = "MS", gel = NA, time = rep(c(0, 30, 240, 1440), each = 3))
ms$value <- log2(conc[match(ms$time, times)]) + rnorm(nrow(ms), 0, 0.5)
wbms <- rbind(cbind(wb, absolute = FALSE), cbind(ms, absolute = TRUE))
head(wbms)
```

### Model

A band reads `log2(2^yi + 2^(b + bj)) + sj`: the log2 concentration `yi` in nM per time
point plus the background, shifted by `sj` per gel, all on the log2 scale. The log2
background is the fixed `b`, common to all gels, plus `bj`, a normal random effect around
0 per gel. A mass spectrometry reading is `yi` itself. The error is absolute, one per
method. The data say little about the background: its spread between gels is small, and
the bands hide most of it. A prior keeps the standard deviation of `bj` near 0.3, its log
`omega_bj_bj` normal around $\log 0.3$ with standard deviation 0.3, and a weak one puts `b`
around 1 nM, normal around 0 with standard deviation 2.

```{r}
m <- alignmentModel(wbms, model = "log2(2^yi + 2^(b + bj)) + sj", errmodel = "sigma",
                    biological = yi ~ time,
                    scaling    = list(sj ~ gel, b ~ 1, bj ~ 0 + (1 | gel)),
                    error      = sigma ~ method,
                    trafo = "sigma <- exp(sigma)",
                    prior = constraintL2(mu = c(omega_bj_bj = log(0.3), b = 0),
                                         sigma = c(omega_bj_bj = 0.3, b = 2)))
m
```

### Fit

The values come out as log2 concentrations in nM, also at the time points the mass
spectrometry did not measure:

```{r}
fit <- align(m, fits = 1)
fit
a <- fit$aligned[order(fit$aligned$time), ]
cbind(a[c("time", "estimate", "se")], nM = round(2^a$estimate, 1), simulated = conc[match(a$time, times)])
```

The background in nM and the standard deviations of the two methods on the log2 scale:

```{r}
p <- fit$parameters
round(2^p[["b"]], 2)
c(MS = exp(p[["sigma"]]), WB = exp(p[["sigma"]] + p[["sigma_methodWB"]]))
```

The readings of every gel and of the mass spectrometry before and after the alignment,
one colour per gel. Before it, the bands are in arbitrary units on the scales of their
gels and the mass spectrometry in nM; after it, all are in nM. The absolute readings stay
as they are:

```{r}
s <- fit$scaled
s$gel <- factor(ifelse(s$absolute, "MS", s$gel), c(gels, "MS"))
panel <- c("before: WB [a.u.]", "before: MS [nM]", "after [nM]")
both <- rbind(data.frame(s[c("gel", "method", "time")], reading = s$value,
                         panel = ifelse(s$absolute, panel[2], panel[1])),
              data.frame(s[c("gel", "method", "time")], reading = s$scaled, panel = panel[3]))
both$panel <- factor(both$panel, panel)
```
```{r fig.width = 11, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(both[is.finite(both$reading), ], aes(factor(time), reading, colour = gel, shape = method)) +
  geom_point() + facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  guides(x = guide_axis(angle = 45)) +
  labs(x = "time [min]", y = "log2(conc.)", colour = "gel", shape = "method") +
  scale_color_dMod(palette = "dMod") + theme_dMod()

```
```{r fig.height = 3.5}
plotAligned(fit) + scale_x_sqrt(breaks = times) + guides(x = guide_axis(angle = 45)) +
  labs(x = "time [min]", y = "log2(conc.) [nM]")
```
```{r fig.height = 3}
plotResiduals(fit)
```

### Random background

The standard deviation of the log2 background between gels, and per gel the mode of its
random effect with its conditional standard error. The standard deviation lies near the
mean of its prior: its value comes mostly from the prior, not from the data.

```{r}
fit$omega
fit$random
```

The shrinkage, $1 - \operatorname{SD}(\text{modes}) / \omega$, says how much the data know about
the random effect of a single gel. Where the bands hide the background, the mode of a gel stays
near 0, the population value. The aligned values, `b` and $\omega$ integrate over the random
effects and do not depend on the modes; the mode of a gel is no measurement of its background, and
plots of the modes look too narrow.

```{r}
fit$fit$shrinkage
```

Draws from the conditional distributions of the random effects against the estimated
normal distribution, which they follow whatever the shrinkage. At a high shrinkage the
draws mostly repeat that normal distribution, so the plot could hardly reveal a
background distributed otherwise.

```{r fig.height = 6}
plotRandomEffects(fit$fit)
```

The readings against the individual prediction (IPRED), with the random effects at
their modes, and the population prediction (PRED), with every gel at the population
background:

```{r fig.height = 3.5}
plot(fit$fit) + theme(legend.position = "right") + labs(colour = "gel")
```
